description: Forty-Four Ways to Win the War. Chicago: Marshall Field & Co., September 1918 Contextual Background Published in 1918 during the final year of the First World War, Forty-Four Ways to Win the War was issued by Marshall Field & Company, a prominent Chicago-based department store. The text reflects a pivotal moment in American domestic mobilization, when the U.S. government—through agencies like the U.S. Food Administration led by Herbert Hoover—called on civilians, especially women, to support the war effort through food conservation, substitution, and homefront sacrifice. With American troops fighting alongside the Allies in Europe, and with wartime shortages affecting both military and civilian populations, the government promoted a cultural campaign of voluntary rationing. Slogans like "Food Will Win the War" became widely known, and households were encouraged to observe "Meatless Mondays" and "Wheatless Wednesdays." In this context, department stores like Marshall Field’s played an essential role not only as retailers but as civic institutions—educating, equipping, and encouraging Americans to adopt patriotic consumption habits. The booklet serves as both a wartime cookbook and a promotional catalogue. It features recipes using alternative grains (like cornmeal, rye, and barley) and substitutes for sugar, meat, and dairy—commodities needed overseas. Simultaneously, it markets domestic appliances such as waffle irons, cereal grinders, and fireless cookers as tools of efficient, modern, and loyal housekeeping. The tone of the publication blends patriotism with commercial appeal, targeting the American homemaker as a central figure in national defense. Women were urged to see their kitchens as frontlines and their food choices as military contributions. The inclusion of institutional endorsements, such as acknowledgments to university circulars and U.S. Department of Agriculture pamphlets, gives the publication an air of civic responsibility, even as it promotes consumer products. Forty-Four Ways to Win the War stands as a unique historical artifact—part cookbook, part propaganda, part marketing—revealing how American businesses adapted to and participated in the national war effort through appeals to duty, domesticity, and innovation. Thematic Summary Theme 1: Civilian Mobilization and Total War The booklet exemplifies how World War I transformed civilian life into a vital component of the war effort. The concept of "total war" —where entire societies mobilize economically, socially, and ideologically to support military campaigns—is central to this text. Women are especially positioned as frontline contributors through their domestic labor, food preparation, and commitment to rationing and substitution. IB Link : Authoritarian and democratic state mobilization strategies; wartime propaganda and social policies. APUSH / AP World Link : Homefront mobilization during WWI; societal shifts during global conflict.   Theme 2: Food as a Weapon of War A dominant theme is the weaponization of food . The conservation and substitution of wheat, meat, dairy, and sugar are portrayed as essential acts of patriotism. Recipes use barley, rye, cornmeal, and hominy in place of wheat. Meat is limited or eliminated in many meals. Sugar is rationed to support Allied needs. Food becomes a moral, strategic, and national resource. IB Link : Economic and social impacts of war on civilian populations. AP Link : Wartime rationing and the U.S. Food Administration under Hoover.   Theme 3: Gender Roles and Domestic Patriotism The text implicitly and explicitly defines women as the moral guardians of the home front , responsible for adapting their kitchens and lifestyles to national goals. While men fight abroad, women’s contribution is framed as equally vital. This anticipates broader changes in gender roles and highlights women's evolving public presence during wartime. IB Link : Gender roles in war and society. AP Link : Women's roles during WWI; the origins of women’s increased civic engagement and suffrage activism.   Theme 4: Consumer Culture and Wartime Commerce Though patriotic in tone, the booklet is also a department store catalogue. It blends war propaganda with consumerism , promoting modern kitchen appliances and tools as instruments of patriotic service. The intersection of capitalism and national duty reflects how private enterprise participated in state mobilization and shaped wartime culture. IB Link : Economic policy and propaganda; the role of media and commerce in shaping public opinion. AP Link : Wartime propaganda, industrial production, and the homefront economy.   Theme 5: National Identity and Sacrifice Throughout the text, readers are reminded that America's allies depend on them. Emotional appeals frame American identity as tied to sacrifice, unity, and moral leadership . The household is imagined as a battlefield of discipline and devotion, reinforcing nationalism through daily acts. IB Link : Nationalism, identity, and propaganda. AP Link : War and American national identity in the early 20th century. Description Forty-Four Ways to Win the War is a World War I-era homefront cookbook and commercial pamphlet published in 1918 by Marshall Field & Company, a major department store in Chicago. The booklet offers wartime recipes, food conservation strategies, and household advice aimed at American women, who were called upon to support the Allied war effort through mindful cooking, rationing, and substitution of scarce ingredients like wheat, meat, and sugar. Blending patriotic messaging with product advertisements for kitchen tools, the text reflects the broader wartime theme of total civilian mobilization , where domestic life was reframed as a front line in the struggle to secure victory. It promotes the idea that home economics, sacrifice, and everyday consumer choices were integral to national defense , making the home kitchen a site of civic duty and strategic importance. OPCVL With reference to its origin, Forty-Four Ways to Win the War was published in 1918 by Marshall Field & Company, a prominent Chicago department store, during the final year of World War I. Its primary purpose was to educate and encourage American civilians—especially women—to contribute to the Allied war effort by conserving food at home. The content includes 44 wartime recipes that substitute scarce goods like wheat, meat, and sugar with alternatives such as cornmeal, barley, and honey. The text reflects government-endorsed conservation campaigns led by the U.S. Food Administration, but it is also a commercial catalogue that promotes modern kitchen appliances as tools of patriotic housekeeping. For a history student or political scientist, this duality offers valuable insight into how public policy goals—such as rationing and civilian mobilization—were disseminated not only through official channels, but also through private enterprise and consumer culture. However, the source also presents limitations. It reflects a middle- to upper-class, urban, and consumerist perspective that may not represent the experiences of rural Americans, working-class households, or ethnic minorities. The document assumes access to store-bought appliances and a well-equipped kitchen, overlooking structural inequalities that affected participation in homefront policies. Additionally, its promotional tone may obscure the coercive or compulsory aspects of wartime rationing and overlooks dissent or fatigue on the home front. While it powerfully illustrates the role of gendered domestic labor in national strategy and offers evidence of how war reshaped private life, it should be supplemented with government records, propaganda posters, and personal diaries to develop a more comprehensive view of domestic wartime policy and its social impact. Lenses Historical Theory Lenses Social History The booklet is a prime example of bottom-up social history , focusing on the daily lives and behaviors of civilians, especially women, during wartime. Rather than emphasizing political leaders or military battles, it reveals how ordinary people were mobilized as active participants in the war through domestic labor and consumption choices. This approach aligns with social historians’ interest in non-combatant contributions , gender roles, and the cultural transformations induced by war. Total War Theory From a military-historical standpoint, the document illustrates the theory of total war , in which entire societies—not just armies—are engaged in the war effort. The homefront becomes militarized not through force but through moral persuasion, patriotic messaging, and government-linked civilian initiatives. The text shows how non-combatant spaces like kitchens were reframed as extensions of the battlefield. Gender History The booklet operates within a gendered historical lens by positioning female domestic labor as a form of civic patriotism . It frames women’s culinary decisions as politically and nationally consequential, reinforcing both the gender norms of the era and their evolving public role during wartime. Civic Duty Lenses Republican Civic Virtue The text draws heavily on the civic republican ideal that citizens—particularly women in their domestic role—have a moral obligation to subordinate personal interests to the common good in times of crisis. Cooking with cornmeal or abstaining from sugar becomes not just a practical act, but a virtuous one tied to the survival of the republic and its allies. Progressive-Era Social Efficiency Reflecting Progressive Era values , the booklet merges patriotism with consumer efficiency and scientific home management. It implies that loyalty to the nation is demonstrated through rationalized, measured, and hygienic domestic labor. Civic duty is thus intertwined with modernity, productiveness, and moral self-regulation. Propaganda and Participatory Nationalism The text fits within a civic lens of participatory nationalism , encouraging voluntary compliance with national food policies through emotional appeals and the illusion of consumer empowerment. It promotes a cooperative model of citizenship in which civilians share responsibility for national outcomes through everyday behaviors.   Together, these lenses reveal how Forty-Four Ways to Win the War is not merely a cookbook, but a civic artifact that fused nationalism, gender roles, consumerism, and wartime governance into a unified ideological message of patriotic duty in the kitchen. Key Themes & Discussion Points Homefront as Battlefield – Civilian kitchens reframed as sites of national defense and patriotic action. Gender and Civic Duty – Women's roles emphasized as essential in wartime not through military service, but domestic sacrifice. Food as Strategy – Substitution and conservation positioned as acts of political and military significance. Commercial Patriotism – Blurring of consumer culture and national service through product placement and appliance marketing. Propaganda and Voluntary Compliance – The use of moral persuasion and guilt appeals to drive voluntary adherence to wartime policies. Description

Forty-Four Ways to Win the War is a World War I-era homefront cookbook and commercial pamphlet published in 1918 by Marshall Field & Company, a major department store in Chicago. The booklet offers wartime recipes, food conservation strategies, and household advice aimed at American women, who were called upon to support the Allied war effort through mindful cooking, rationing, and substitution of scarce ingredients like wheat, meat, and sugar. It promotes the idea that home economics, sacrifice, and everyday consumer choices were integral to national defense, making the home kitchen a site of civic duty and strategic importance.

OPCVL

With reference to its origin, Forty-Four Ways to Win the War was published in 1918 by Marshall Field & Company, a prominent Chicago department store, during the final year of World War I. Its primary purpose was to educate and encourage American civilians—especially women—to contribute to the Allied war effort by conserving food at home. The content includes 44 wartime recipes that substitute scarce goods like wheat, meat, and sugar with alternatives such as cornmeal, barley, and honey. The text reflects government-endorsed conservation campaigns led by the U.S. Food Administration, but it is also a commercial catalogue that promotes modern kitchen appliances as tools of patriotic housekeeping. For a history student or political scientist, this duality offers valuable insight into how public policy goals—such as rationing and civilian mobilization—were disseminated not only through official channels, but also through private enterprise and consumer culture.

However, the source also presents limitations. It reflects a middle- to upper-class, urban, and consumerist perspective that may not represent the experiences of rural Americans, working-class households, or ethnic minorities. The document assumes access to store-bought appliances and a well-equipped kitchen, overlooking structural inequalities that affected participation in homefront policies. Additionally, its promotional tone may obscure the coercive or compulsory aspects of wartime rationing and overlooks dissent or fatigue on the home front. While it powerfully illustrates the role of gendered domestic labor in national strategy and offers evidence of how war reshaped private life, it should be supplemented with government records, propaganda posters, and personal diaries to develop a more comprehensive view of domestic wartime policy and its social impact.

Lenses

Historical Theory Lenses

  1. Social History
    The booklet is a prime example of bottom-up social history, focusing on the daily lives and behaviors of civilians, especially women, during wartime. Rather than emphasizing political leaders or military battles, it reveals how ordinary people were mobilized as active participants in the war through domestic labor and consumption choices. This approach aligns with social historians’ interest in non-combatant contributions, gender roles, and the cultural transformations induced by war.

  2. Total War Theory
    From a military-historical standpoint, the document illustrates the theory of total war, in which entire societies—not just armies—are engaged in the war effort. The homefront becomes militarized not through force but through moral persuasion, patriotic messaging, and government-linked civilian initiatives. The text shows how non-combatant spaces like kitchens were reframed as extensions of the battlefield.

  3. Gender History
    The booklet operates within a gendered historical lens by positioning female domestic labor as a form of civic patriotism. It frames women’s culinary decisions as politically and nationally consequential, reinforcing both the gender norms of the era and their evolving public role during wartime.

Civic Duty Lenses

  1. Republican Civic Virtue
    The text draws heavily on the civic republican ideal that citizens—particularly women in their domestic role—have a moral obligation to subordinate personal interests to the common good in times of crisis. Cooking with cornmeal or abstaining from sugar becomes not just a practical act, but a virtuous one tied to the survival of the republic and its allies.

  2. Progressive-Era Social Efficiency
    Reflecting Progressive Era values, the booklet merges patriotism with consumer efficiency and scientific home management. It implies that loyalty to the nation is demonstrated through rationalized, measured, and hygienic domestic labor. Civic duty is thus intertwined with modernity, productiveness, and moral self-regulation.

  3. Propaganda and Participatory Nationalism
    The text fits within a civic lens of participatory nationalism, encouraging voluntary compliance with national food policies through emotional appeals and the illusion of consumer empowerment. It promotes a cooperative model of citizenship in which civilians share responsibility for national outcomes through everyday behaviors.

 

Together, these lenses reveal how Forty-Four Ways to Win the War is not merely a cookbook, but a civic artifact that fused nationalism, gender roles, consumerism, and wartime governance into a unified ideological message of patriotic duty in the kitchen.

Key Themes & Discussion Points

  1. Homefront as Battlefield – Civilian kitchens reframed as sites of national defense and patriotic action.

  2. Gender and Civic Duty – Women's roles emphasized as essential in wartime not through military service, but domestic sacrifice.

  3. Food as Strategy – Substitution and conservation positioned as acts of political and military significance.

  4. Commercial Patriotism – Blurring of consumer culture and national service through product placement and appliance marketing.

  5. Propaganda and Voluntary Compliance – The use of moral persuasion and guilt appeals to drive voluntary adherence to wartime policies.

Quote Bank for Analysis or Essay Prompts

Each quote is followed by a prompt you can use for AP FRQs, IB Paper 2/3 essays, or internal assessments:

“Wars are not won by battles alone... every ounce of meat or wheat or sweet that we save in our kitchens is calculating conservation.”
Discuss how this quote illustrates the concept of total war and how non-combatants were mobilized as strategic assets.

“Patriotism and food! Winning a world war by eating corn and chicken instead of wheat and beef!”
Evaluate how food choices were politicized as moral acts during World War I.

“Every flag that flies opposite the German flag is flying in our defense.”
Analyze the role of nationalism in shaping civilian attitudes and actions during global conflict.

“Use less fried foods and save fats… the importation of oils from Africa, South America and Asia has almost entirely ceased.”
Explore the economic dimensions of war-related scarcity and its influence on civilian behavior.

Curricular Alignment & Use Cases

IB History (Paper 2 & 3)

  • Prescribed Subject: Rights and Protest (gender roles, civil duty)

  • World History Topic: The Move to Global War / Authoritarian States – propaganda and mobilization

  • HL Americas: U.S. homefront during WWI; mobilization and social transformation

IB Global Politics

  • Human Rights & Development: Gendered division of labor, food security

  • Peace & Conflict: Total war, civilian-military interaction

AP U.S. History (APUSH)

  • Period 7 (1890–1945): WWI homefront, Herbert Hoover’s Food Administration, voluntary rationing

  • Themes: Politics and Power, American and National Identity, Work/Exchange/Technology

AP World History: Modern

  • Unit 7: Global Conflict – total war, wartime propaganda, civilian mobilization

  • Themes: State-building, Economic Systems, Cultural Developments

Extended Essay or IA Research Potential

IB History EE or IA Topics

  • To what extent did voluntary food conservation policies shape public attitudes toward national service in the United States during WWI?

  • How effectively did gendered propaganda influence women's roles on the U.S. homefront during World War I?

AP Research

  • How did department stores serve as conduits for patriotic messaging during World War I?

  • To what extent did consumer behavior change as a result of civilian mobilization efforts in the U.S. during WWI?

Key Excerpts + Annotations (with Vocabulary Support)

“We must save for them. Use less fried foods and save fats… the importation of oils… has ceased.”
Annotation: Reflects scarcity-driven moral economy. Fats, normally overlooked, become wartime commodities.
Vocabulary: Importation – bringing goods in from abroad. Scarcity – limited supply; moral economy – economic behavior shaped by social values.

“Food will win the war.”
Annotation: Hoover's slogan used to mobilize domestic kitchens. Illustrates reduction of warfare to civic behavior.
Vocabulary: Mobilize – to organize or prepare for action; slogan – short, memorable phrase used in propaganda.

“Crackling bread… because of its large percentage of fat… should be served very hot.”
Annotation: Practical adaptation of regional (Southern) recipes to meet conservation needs.

Suggested Writing Prompts

IB-Style Extended Essay Practice

  • Evaluate the extent to which American domestic food policy during WWI relied on voluntary rather than coercive mechanisms.

  • In what ways did department stores and commercial media support government mobilization campaigns in democratic states during World War I?

AP Free Response Practice

  • Analyze the ways in which the U.S. government and private sector collaborated to influence civilian behavior during World War I.

  • Explain how wartime conditions altered the relationship between American women and the state during World War I.

Mr. Hutchings’ Suggestions (Scholarly Extensions)

“Nothing is so strongly fortified that it cannot be taken by strategy or by love.”
Use this as a metaphor to explore how Forty-Four Ways represents a soft form of wartime mobilization—strategic, persuasive, and infused with patriotic affection.

Consider comparative lenses:
Study this pamphlet alongside:

  • British WWI food propaganda (e.g. Ministry of Food posters)

  • Soviet WWII cookbooks and domestic manuals

  • WWII-era Japanese homefront mobilization of women

Interdisciplinary Dialogue:
Bridge political theory with economic sociology: How do texts like this reflect Foucault’s ideas of biopolitics—where state power is exerted through control of food, health, and domestic behavior?

Critical Reflection Question:
Was voluntary rationing truly voluntary, or was it driven by social pressure, propaganda, and gender norms? What are the boundaries between patriotism and propaganda?
